source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: Chunking is a recorder of goal-based experience. When a subgoal ends, Soar builds one production that returns the subgoal's result next time the same situation appears. No separate analysis step is run.
numbers: Tasks: Eight Puzzle, Tic-Tac-Toe, part of R1 (configuration). Claims four contributions: speed-up, all aspects of behaviour, transfer, strategy acquisition.
quote: Chunking is well suited to be such a learning mechanism because it is a recorder of goal-based experience
limits: Early demonstration. Qualitative figures for Eight Puzzle and Tic-Tac-Toe, numbers only for R1-Soar.
agent_relevance: A lesson written after a sub-problem ends, triggered by the sub-problem finishing, not by a schedule. Matches the S6 subgoal return.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: How a chunk is built. Soar keeps a condition list per goal: every datum that existed before the goal and was accessed by a firing production. Conditions are those data, variablized so two variables cannot match one object. Actions are the subgoal results, pruned to what connects to a supergoal.
numbers: Data counts as accessed if a production that matched it fires. One production per terminated subgoal (the earlier psychology model used three: encode, map, decode).
quote: The conditions of a chunked production need to test everything that was used in creating the results of the subgoal
limits: Condition list is built from what was used, not what was true. Anything the reasoning might have used but did not is absent.
agent_relevance: For a stored lesson, record the precondition as only the facts actually consulted. That gives free generality and also the over-general risk in a06.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: Implicit generalization: chunks contain only the aspects accessed in the subgoal, so irrelevant context is ignored automatically. This yields transfer without any generalizing algorithm.
numbers: Eight Puzzle: one learning run removed search entirely on the same task (after-learning column). A different task (different start and goal, no shared intermediate states) learned first, then task 1 re-run with learning off: search still reduced, showing across-task transfer.
limits: Eight Puzzle figures are drawn graphs, no exact counts in the text. Two operator choices were set by hand because the evaluation function was too weak. Search control forbids undoing the last move.
agent_relevance: Transfer comes from stating what a helper actually needs, not from a larger library. Test on a second, different problem sharing sub-problems.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: R1-Soar (configuration expert system) shows large speed-up from chunking inside one run and after one run.
numbers: Minimal search control (232 productions): 1731 decisions without chunking; 485 decisions and 59 new productions with chunking in the same run; 7 decisions on rerun. With 10 hand-written search-control rules (242 productions): 150 decisions; 90 with chunking; 7 on rerun.
limits: Rerun is the identical task, so 7 decisions is a caching result. Chunking adds about 15 percent run-time overhead (the footnote OCR reads 1546; read as 15 percent). 1 second per decision on a Symbolics 3600.
agent_relevance: Learning in the same run (within-trial transfer) gave 1731 to 485, a 3.6x drop, before any second attempt. Lessons can pay off inside one problem.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: Tic-Tac-Toe: chunks detect board symmetries without being told about symmetry, because they ignore orientation information that was never used. Chunks also store the right moves (strategy acquisition).
numbers: Qualitative: symmetric positions no longer re-explored. No counts given.
limits: Only the basic problem space (board, who moves, win/loss/draw detection) was coded. Quality of the learned path depends on quality of the problem solving, not on the learning.
agent_relevance: A stored lesson is only as good as the search that produced it (consistent with G3: a pass must be on something not fitted).

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1984) Towards Chunking as a General Learning Mechanism
finding: Over-general chunk found in the founding paper. Special-case knowledge that was almost used (most conditions satisfied, not all) is not recorded, so the chunk fires where the special case should have overridden it.
numbers: Tic-Tac-Toe example: O has centre, X on a side. Tie among 7 moves. Chunk tests marks at A, B, C, E, I and clear squares G, F, but not D or H. In a later state with X at D the chunk still proposes I, which loses.
quote: Over-generalization is a serious problem for Soar if we want to encode real tasks that are able to improve with experience.
limits: Authors call it a serious problem and a source of negative transfer. Their proposed fix, learning new chunks that override the bad one, is future work.
agent_relevance: Direct warning for any lesson library: store the near-miss conditions or the lesson can fire in the wrong context. Gate with a held-out check (G3).

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by Chunking: Summary of a Task and a Model
finding: Chunking theory of learning rests on three assumptions: Performance (higher-level chunks process faster than their parts; needs a serial bottleneck plus a parallel component); Learning (chunks acquired at constant average rate from patterns met); Task-structure (probability a pattern recurs falls as pattern size grows).
numbers: Power law T = B N^-a, known since Snoddy (1926). Chunk = encoding, mapping and decoding production.
quote: Practice consists of the acquisition of these patterns from tasks already performed.
limits: This is a macro-theory plus one implemented micro-model. The power law is derived from the three assumptions, not fitted.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable reason why returns diminish: big lessons recur rarely. Predicts the skill library should show diminishing returns per added item.

source: Rosenbloom & Newell (1982) Learning by Chunking: Summary of a Task and a Model
finding: Model of Seibel's 1023-choice reaction task in the Xaps2 production system. Learning adds a chunk whenever two successively fixated patterns occur in one trial. A faster meta-model simulates the cycles.
numbers: Task: 10 lights, 10 buttons, 1023 stimulus patterns. Human data: 76,725 trials show a power law. Meta-model cost: 13 cycles per trial plus 31 cycles per pattern used. Simulated 72,633 trials gave a straight line on log-log axes.
limits: Detailed model only run on 9 trials (left hand, five lights). A chunk was learned with fixed probability 0.01 because learning at every chance would finish the task in about 3 to 4 passes. Method acquisition not modelled. Fitted constant in the printed equation is garbled in the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Learning-rate parameter was set by hand to get the curve, so the power law is partly an assumed constant rate, not an independent confirmation.

source: Newell & Rosenbloom (1981) Mechanisms of skill acquisition and the law of practice
finding: Original statement of the power law across the full range of human tasks and the chunking explanation. Not read directly; known only through citations in a07, a08 and Wikipedia.
numbers: Cited as pp. 1-55 in Anderson (ed.) Cognitive Skills and Their Acquisition.
limits: Original text not opened. Detail on the number of tasks fitted is unverified.
agent_relevance: Do not cite numbers from this paper until opened.

source: Wikipedia: Power law of practice (secondary summary)
finding: Gives the two competing curve forms and the aggregation-artifact argument. Heathcote, Brown & Mewhort (2000): the power function in averaged curves is an artifact of averaging; individual data fit an exponential better.
numbers: Power: RT = a*P^-b + c. Exponential: RT = a*e^(-b(P-1)) + c. Latency = A + B*T^d for retention.
limits: Page gives no fitted exponents or sample sizes. Snoddy date is inconsistent on the page (1926 vs 1928).
agent_relevance: Do not build the schema on a power-law promise for stored lessons. Expect fast early gain then a plateau, shape unknown.

source: Heathcote, Brown, Mewhort (2000) The power law repealed: the case for an exponential law of practice
finding: Fit power and exponential functions to individual learners across many published datasets. Exponential won in every unaveraged dataset. Averaging produces a power-law bias.
numbers: 40 datasets, 7910 learning series, 475 subjects, 24 experiments (from a search abstract). APEX function (exponential with a pre-experimental practice parameter) also introduced.
limits: Figures taken from a search summary, not read in full. Direct challenge to the data behind the chunking account of the power law (see a07).
agent_relevance: If Soar agents or LLM libraries are plotted, fit per run, not on the average.

source: Doorenbos, Tambe, Newell (1992) Learning 10,000 chunks: what's it like out there?
finding: Largest chunking run reported at the time: Dispatcher-Soar learned 10,112 chunks over 200 random dispatching problems. The chunk rate stayed constant, matching the Learning Assumption in a07.
numbers: Start 1,819 productions, end 11,931. One chunk per 6.3 decision cycles; 20.5 production firings per decision cycle; 130 firings per chunk. First problem 3,143 decision cycles and 556 chunks. Mix of chunks: about 30% search control, 32% operator implementation, 38% memorized database query results.
limits: One system, one task domain, Soar 5.2.2 all-goals chunking, 20 problem spaces. Same 1-per-6 rate seen in about 100 chunks in other tasks (Tambe et al. 1990).
agent_relevance: Rate of lesson creation is set by sub-problem count, not by how good the lesson is. Cap or filter lessons rather than keep all.

source: Doorenbos, Tambe, Newell (1992) Learning 10,000 chunks: what's it like out there?
finding: Learning followed a power law on held-out probe problems. 10 probe problems (3 easy, 3 medium, 4 hard) were re-run with the chunks from 0 to 200 base problems; the log-log plot is roughly a straight line.
numbers: Overall speed-up first-to-last trial: factor 7. Early chunks help most; later ones still help less. Only 10.3% of chunks ever transferred to a later base problem. Repeating an identical problem takes 4 decision cycles.
limits: Ten probe problems only. The power-law claim is by eye on a log-log plot (the printed fit is garbled). Transfer share is a lower bound since late chunks had no time to be reused.
agent_relevance: Strong design to copy: measure transfer with fixed disjoint probe problems at each library size, not with the running average.

source: Doorenbos, Tambe, Newell (1992) Learning 10,000 chunks: what's it like out there?
finding: No average growth effect in match cost, against the prediction of the utility problem, but wall-clock time still grows.
numbers: Tokens per decision cycle did not increase over about 65,000 decision cycles and 10,112 chunks (slightly decreasing fit). Time per decision cycle 1.28 s at start, +0.47 s per 10,000 chunks. Rete network size grew eight-fold in interpreted code.
limits: Cause of the missing growth effect was not found; several hypotheses rejected. Held for this system only. Source of time growth unclear.
agent_relevance: In a prompt library the cost is not match time but context tokens and retrieval errors. Measure those directly.

source: Doorenbos, Tambe, Newell (1992) Learning 10,000 chunks: what's it like out there?
finding: Learning effectiveness varies strongly by problem space. Most gain comes from few chunks that transfer often. Child-space chunks can be cut off by parent-space chunks firing first.
numbers: Percent of chunks that transfer ranged from 0% to 100% by space. 42 of 200 problems solved without consulting the database. rrep-for-ent space built 55 chunks, none ever transferred. 87% of pathfinder chunks built in first half of run.
limits: Percentages are per problem space in one system.
agent_relevance: Expect a long tail of unused lessons. Retire a lesson never retrieved, and prefer lessons at the highest level that fires.

source: Tambe, Newell, Rosenbloom (1990) The problem of expensive chunks and its solution by restricting expressiveness
finding: A single chunk can cost so much to match that it erases the savings, because the condition list can express a hard match. Fix: restrict the language of conditions so match effort is bounded. Abstract only, from a search summary; not read.
numbers: Abstract: expensive chunks exist, their causes are analysed, a restricted-expressiveness fix is proposed with trade-offs and empirical evidence. Machine Learning 5, pp. 299-348.
limits: Full text blocked (Springer login redirect). No numbers verified.
agent_relevance: Lessons should have a bounded form. In prompts, a long conditional lesson can cost more tokens than the search it saves.

source: Rosenbloom & Aasman (1990) Knowledge level and inductive uses of chunking (EBL)
finding: Soar chunking is a variant of explanation-based learning and can also do rote memorization and induction. Hypothesis: rote learning, empirical generalization and EBL are variations of one knowledge-reconstruction process. Implemented a task-independent rote memory and a version-space inductive learner using chunks.
numbers: Version space stored as rules; concept learned from several examples in Soar.
quote: Rote learning, empirical generalization, and explanation-based learning arise as variations in the knowledge-reconstruction process
limits: Needs the non-penetrable memory assumption (Soar cannot read its own rules), which complicates induction. Proof of concept on toy concept tasks.
agent_relevance: Chunking by itself is deductive and adds no new facts. New knowledge about what works must come from tested examples, which is the point of G3.

source: Mitchell, Keller, Kedar-Cabelli (1986) Explanation-based generalization: a unifying view
finding: EBG forms a general concept from one example by explaining why the example belongs to the concept using domain knowledge, then generalizing the explanation. Unifies earlier systems. Only the abstract page was read.
numbers: No experiments in the abstract. Springer PDF link given.
limits: Abstract-level only. The approach needs a correct domain theory.
agent_relevance: The theory is a proof that a lesson is valid. An LLM has no sound domain theory, so any lesson from it needs an executable check.

source: Laird, Rosenbloom, Newell (1986) Chunking in Soar: the anatomy of a general learning mechanism
finding: Journal analysis of how chunking works inside Soar, showing it learning and using macro-operators and learning search control and operator implementation rules. Only the abstract page was read.
numbers: Abstract only. Machine Learning 1:11-46.
limits: Full text not obtained (DTIC and Springer PDFs not retrievable here). Details come from the 1984 predecessor in a01 to a06.
agent_relevance: Same as a01.

source: Laird, Newell, Rosenbloom (1987) Soar: an architecture for general intelligence (summary by J. Davies)
finding: Uniform learning hypothesis: goal-based chunking is the general learning mechanism. Chunking learns to avoid the impasses that created subgoals. The summary lists as not yet possible: recovery from overgeneralized learning and further learning types.
numbers: No experiments or numbers in the summary.
limits: Secondary summary of a long paper; not the paper.
agent_relevance: The impasse-then-compile loop is the closest match to S6 followed by S9 storing a lesson.

source: Soar Manual (9.6) Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Current definition: chunks are created whenever a subgoal creates a result in a superstate, built as soon as the result appears. Conditions come from backtracing through rule firings to superstate elements tested. Procedural learning is off by default.
numbers: Hundreds of rule firings can compress into one firing. Arithmetic agent: Soar 9.4 learned 1263 specific rules, Soar 9.6 learned 8 general rules.
quote: Chunks are created whenever one subgoal creates a result in a superstate.
limits: Manual text, not an experiment. Rule counts have no stated task size or run count.
agent_relevance: Modern chunking changed from 'only what was accessed' to explanation-based chunking with identity tracking for better generality, at the cost of complexity.

source: Soar Manual (9.6) Procedural Knowledge Learning
finding: Documented ways chunks can be incorrect or over-general, which Soar now filters or flags.
numbers: Over-general = applies where original problem-solving would never occur. Sources: local negations on substate data, recalled semantic or episodic memory treated as local, tests on impasse existence, random or reinforcement-learned operator choices (no correct chunk possible), RHS function results (forces literal values). Seven stop conditions. allow-local-negations is the only correctness filter in 9.6.0.
limits: Does not give frequency of each problem. add-osk (operator selection knowledge) is off by default.
agent_relevance: Same failure kinds for an LLM lesson library: lessons that relied on a hidden preference, on recalled memory, or on random choice cannot be re-checked and should not be stored as rules.

source: Taatgen & Anderson (2002) Why do children learn to say 'broke'? A model of learning the past tense without feedback
finding: ACT-R production compilation. Two rules that fire in sequence, the first retrieving a chunk, are merged into one rule with the retrieved fact built in, removing the retrieval. A new rule starts with a utility below its parents and extra noise.
numbers: Only learned when parent rules have enough experience; new rules are not built from newly learned rules. First rule takes about one simulated month. Model gives U-shaped learning, and still learns the regular rule when regular verbs are under 10% type frequency and 5% token frequency.
quote: The circumstance for learning a new production rule is that two rules fire one after another with the first rule retrieving a chunk from memory.
limits: One domain (English past tense), simulation compared with child data. The stochastic utility competition is what makes the rule slowly take over.
agent_relevance: A new lesson should enter at lower trust than its source and earn its way up by measured use, which is a version of G7.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition
finding: Production compilation replaces ACT* knowledge compilation (proceduralization plus composition, generalization, specialization). Anderson dropped the old version in 1998 for lack of evidence and 'computational misbehavior' (loops, early aborts, too many chances to learn faulty rules).
numbers: Model of the Kanfer-Ackerman air traffic controller task with default ACT-R parameters. Fit to 65 undergraduates, 18 ten-minute trials; model compared on trials 1 to 10: r squared = .97 for planes landed.
limits: Model starts with all declarative knowledge, so it beats people on the first trials. Fit is on group means. Early human gain is also attributed to learning the screen layout.
agent_relevance: The paper notes Soar and ACT* macro-procedures got too large to match (Tambe et al. 1990) and too unconstrained. Merging only two steps at a time is the guard; good model for small composable lessons.

source: Taatgen & Lee (2003) Production compilation: a simple mechanism to model complex skill acquisition
finding: Overgeneralization in production compilation is blamed on the strategy of reusing old experience, not on the mechanism. Compilation never produces rules unrelated to existing ones.
numbers: Example rule for landing a plane combines an instruction-retrieval step with a motor step; the compiled rule fires directly.
limits: Argued by the authors; no separate test of how often faulty rules are made.
agent_relevance: Learned procedures should be derived from existing, tested ones and not created from nothing.

source: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) An open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Skill library of executable code, stored after self-verification and retrieved by description, is the LLM analogue of chunks. No weights change. It was the main source of late-stage gain.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior best. Tech tree (iterations, 3 runs, cap 160): Voyager wooden 6+-2, stone 11+-2, iron 21+-7; AutoGPT 92+-72, 94+-72, 135+-103; ReAct and Reflexion 0 of 3 on all levels.
limits: Only 3 runs per method. GPT-4 needed: GPT-3.5 for code gets 5.7x fewer unique items. Hallucinated tasks and invalid code API calls remain.
agent_relevance: Ablation without skill library plateaus late. Automatic curriculum off: -93% items; self-verification off: -73% items; so the verified-store gate matters more than the store.

source: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023) zero-shot transfer
finding: Transfer test: in a fresh Minecraft world with unseen tasks, a learned library helps. Table 2, cap 50 iterations, 3 attempts.
numbers: Voyager solved all 4 unseen tasks 3 of 3: diamond pickaxe 19+-3, golden sword 18+-7, lava bucket 21+-5 iterations. ReAct, Reflexion, plain AutoGPT 0 of 3. AutoGPT given Voyager's library: diamond pickaxe 1/3, golden sword 1/3, compass 2/3, lava bucket 0/3. Voyager without skill library: diamond pickaxe 2/3 at 36, others 3/3 at 26 to 30.
limits: Three attempts each. Transfer is to the same game with the same primitives. The library helps a weaker loop only partly, so loop and library are coupled. Column mapping read from garbled table text.
agent_relevance: The library without the verification and iteration loop gave only 4 of 12 task successes against 12 of 12. Store and loop must both be copied.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Workflow memory: induce reusable sub-routines from successful trajectories (abstracting example-specific values), put them in memory, online or offline. A direct chunking analogue with measured transfer.
numbers: WebArena, GPT-4 temp 0, online: total success 35.5% vs BrowserGym baseline 23.5% (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative); +7.6% relative over SteP with human-written workflows; 2.0 fewer steps than BrowserGym and 40.8 fewer than AutoEval.
limits: Single model. Workflows induced only from successes judged by an LLM evaluator, so wrong labels can enter memory.
agent_relevance: Online induction needs no extra data. Gains came from selective use of routines, not full replays.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Mind2Web generalization (GPT-4): gain is large on step level and element choice, small on whole-task success. Online beats offline as the gap to training data widens.
numbers: Cross-task: element accuracy 41.6 to 50.6, step success 36.2 to 45.1, task success 2.0 to 4.8 (offline). Cross-domain step success 18.6 baseline, 32.6 offline, 35.5 online; task success 1.0, 0.7, 1.7. Action F1 fell 60.6 to 57.3 cross-task.
limits: Task success rates are 5% or less, so those differences are 1 to 3 points on tiny base counts. Workflows may bias actions that do not fit the state at hand (F1 loss).
agent_relevance: Evidence that a transferred routine can mislead: report step-level and task-level together, and check action fit.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Abstract sub-routine form versus plain stored trajectories. LLM-induced workflows beat rule-based dedup of action sequences mainly on Mind2Web; roughly tied on WebArena.
numbers: WebArena: rule 35.6% with 6.3 steps vs LLM 35.5% with 5.9 steps. Mind2Web cross-task: rule step success 43.4, task 2.0; LLM 45.1, 4.8. Code vs text workflows: 45.1/4.8 vs 45.4/3.6.
limits: Differences of 0.1 to 2.8 points on single runs; no confidence intervals reported.
agent_relevance: Abstracting away example-specific values is what keeps a lesson general, like variablizing chunk conditions in a02.

source: ASI and SkillWeaver (2025) skill induction for web agents (search summaries only)
finding: Follow-up skill libraries: programmatic skills verified by execution. Reported in search summaries, not opened.
numbers: ASI (arXiv 2504.06821) reported +23.5% success vs a static baseline on WebArena and 10.7 to 15.3% fewer steps; SkillWeaver (2504.07079) +31.8% and +39.8% relative, and up to +54.3% when skills made by a strong agent were given to weaker ones.
limits: Numbers come from secondary summaries, unverified. Baselines differ.
agent_relevance: Strongest sign that verified, executable lessons transfer between models; open and check in Angle B.
